item.title: China lays out plans to land astronauts on the moon 'before 2030.' Can NASA still win this race?
item.description: null China has given us some details about the epic moon landing it plans to pull off a few years from now. Chinese officials laid out the roadmap for its crewed lunar campaign at the 7th Manned Space Symposium, which was held Oct. 31 and Nov. 1 in Beijing. The campaign consists of four missions, culminating in a crewed touchdown "before 2030," according to media reports . That timeline — which is consistent with previous statements made by the China Manned Space Agency — keeps the pressure on the U.S., which aims to put its own astronauts down on the moon in 2028, via NASA's Artemis program . Leaked slide confirms the four-mission progression toward China’s crewed lunar landing:🚀2027: Maiden flight of Long March 10A carrying Mengzhou CSS cargo resupply mission, to validate the new human-rated vehicle and Mengzhou’s orbital operations in LEO.🚀2028: First flight of the heavier CZ-10 with an uncrewed Lanyue lander performing a lunar descent and ascent test, exercising the lander’s propulsion and guidance.🚀🚀2029: Dual CZ-10 launches of Mengzhou and Lanyue for a full-scale lunar-orbit rehearsal, demonstrating rendezvous, docking, and integrated operations.🚀🚀Before the end of 2030: Dual CZ-10 crewed lunar landing mission. November 1, 2026 China shooting for the moon The first mission in China's four-part lunar campaign is scheduled to fly in 2027, according to CNSpaceflight , an X account that keeps a close eye on China's activities in space. The outlet cited an X user who shared a presentation slide of the plan. That launch — the first of of China's new Long March 10A rocket — will send an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO) for a series of tests. Mengzhou , whose name means "Dream Vessel," is the next-gen crew capsule that will carry Chinese astronauts to lunar orbit. Mission number two, launching in 2028, will involve a different set of hardware — the more powerful Long March 10 rocket and the Lanyue ("Embracing the Moon") lunar lander. This will also be an uncrewed flight, and it will mark the debut of the Long March 10, which will send Lanyue to orbit around the moon. If all goes to plan, Lanyue will touch down on the moon and then launch itself back to lunar orbit. Mission number three, flying in 2029, will also target an uncrewed lunar landing, but it will feature two Long March 10 launches — one apiece for Mengzhou and Lanyue. The two spacecraft will conduct a rendezvous and docking rehearsal in lunar orbit, then separate for Lanyue's trip down to the surface. This will set the stage for mission four — the real deal, in which two Long March 10s launch a crewed Mengzhou and an uncrewed Lanyue "before 2030." The two vessels will dock in lunar orbit, and the astronauts will move into Lanyue for their historic lunar landing. Three astronauts will apparently launch on Mengzhou, and two of them will land on the moon aboard Lanyue, according to CNSpaceflight . The duo will spend three days on the lunar surface, conducting moonwalks
item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null China has given us some details about the epic moon landing it plans to pull off a few years from now. Chinese officials laid out the roadmap for its crewed lunar campaign at the 7th Manned Space Symposium, which was held Oct. 31 and Nov. 1 in Beijing. The campaign consists of four missions, culminating in a crewed touchdown "before 2030," according to media reports . That timeline — which is consistent with previous statements made by the China Manned Space Agency — keeps the pressure on the U.S., which aims to put its own astronauts down on the moon in 2028, via NASA's Artemis program . Leaked slide confirms the four-mission progression toward China’s crewed lunar landing:🚀2027: Maiden flight of Long March 10A carrying Mengzhou CSS cargo resupply mission, to validate the new human-rated vehicle and Mengzhou’s orbital operations in LEO.🚀2028: First flight of the heavier CZ-10 with an uncrewed Lanyue lander performing a lunar descent and ascent test, exercising the lander’s propulsion and guidance.🚀🚀2029: Dual CZ-10 launches of Mengzhou and Lanyue for a full-scale lunar-orbit rehearsal, demonstrating rendezvous, docking, and integrated operations.🚀🚀Before the end of 2030: Dual CZ-10 crewed lunar landing mission. November 1, 2026 China shooting for the moon The first mission in China's four-part lunar campaign is scheduled to fly in 2027, according to CNSpaceflight , an X account that keeps a close eye on China's activities in space. The outlet cited an X user who shared a presentation slide of the plan. That launch — the first of of China's new Long March 10A rocket — will send an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO) for a series of tests. Mengzhou , whose name means "Dream Vessel," is the next-gen crew capsule that will carry Chinese astronauts to lunar orbit. Mission number two, launching in 2028, will involve a different set of hardware — the more powerful Long March 10 rocket and the Lanyue ("Embracing the Moon") lunar lander. This will also be an uncrewed flight, and it will mark the debut of the Long March 10, which will send Lanyue to orbit around the moon. If all goes to plan, Lanyue will touch down on the moon and then launch itself back to lunar orbit. Mission number three, flying in 2029, will also target an uncrewed lunar landing, but it will feature two Long March 10 launches — one apiece for Mengzhou and Lanyue. The two spacecraft will conduct a rendezvous and docking rehearsal in lunar orbit, then separate for Lanyue's trip down to the surface. This will set the stage for mission four — the real deal, in which two Long March 10s launch a crewed Mengzhou and an uncrewed Lanyue "before 2030." The two vessels will dock in lunar orbit, and the astronauts will move into Lanyue for their historic lunar landing. Three astronauts will apparently launch on Mengzhou, and two of them will land on the moon aboard Lanyue, according to CNSpaceflight . The duo will spend three days on the lunar surface, conducting moonwalks on each of those days. And about that "before 2030" timeline: The wording may have been chosen very carefully. "One reading is that 2029 coincides with the 80th anniversary of the current government, creating a strong internal incentive to achieve the landing that year. At the same time, the technical schedule (new Long March 10 family, Mengzhou, Lanyue, dual-launch operations) remains aggressive; committing publicly to 2029 would create significant political exposure if any major test slips," CNSpaceflight wrote in a Nov. 2 X post . "Using 'before 2030' therefore functions as deliberate wording flexibility: a 2029 landing can still be presented as an early historic success, while a slip into 2030 remains inside the stated goal without requiring a formal target revision. You just need to put 'year-end' after 'before 2030,'" the outlet added. NASA's plan NASA's Artemis program has already sent astronauts around the moon, doing so this past April on the Artemis II mission. The agency is currently gearing up for Artemis III, a crewed flight to LEO that will test rendezvous and docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's two private crewed landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon . Artemis III is currently on track to fly in the summer of 2027, NASA officials have said. But an on-time liftoff is far from guaranteed, as both Starship and Blue Moon still have some boxes to check. Starship just reached Earth orbit for the first time on Sept. 28 , for example, and it has yet to demonstrate off-Earth refueling , which will be a crucial part of any Starship mission beyond Earth orbit. And Blue Moon has yet to leave the ground at all. The Blue Origin lander is scheduled to fly for the first time next spring, on an uncrewed test mission that will send it to the lunar surface. If all goes well on Artemis III, NASA will be clear to start prepping for Artemis IV, which will put astronauts down near the lunar south pole aboard either Starship or Blue Moon. (It's unclear at the moment which lander NASA will choose.) NASA is currently targeting early 2028 for the launch of Artemis IV. If that schedule holds, the agency will beat China and pull off the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 back in 1972. But the new moon race won't end there, because this one isn't all about flags and footprints. Both NASA and China aim to build bases on the lunar surface over the next decade or so, setting up humanity's first true outpost on a world beyond Earth. The stakes are high , NASA and U.S. military officials have stressed: Whoever does so first can claim the best spots and get the best access to key lunar resources such as water ice. The leader will also get to establish norms of behavior on the moon, which at the moment is a bit of a Wild West of exploration.

item.title: New York's Queens Public Library battles ransomware crims: Wi-Fi, checkouts, and website go dark
item.description: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly. The disruption has downed QPL's website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, its public Wi-Fi, mobile app, and its digital media services. Renewals are also unavailable, although library users are not charged fines for returning materials late. (Since 2021, In October 2021, QPL, Brooklyn Public Library, and New York Public Library - in an effort to help lower income users from being put off borrowing - permanently killed daily late fines on books and circulating materials .) Each of the library system's 66 locations remains open, including the central library in the Jamaica neighborhood in Queens, but QPL warned: "it will take some time before the library's network and systems are restored." QPL said "certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted," advising visitors to check availability with their local branch via phone, and check the library's social media channels for official updates. "Our IT department is working to resolve the issue, and we will keep you informed,” it said in the statement. It added: "We apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience." No established ransomware group has yet claimed responsibility for the disruption, although attacks on publicly funded institutions rarely lead to lucrative payouts. The British Library's infamous ransomware attack in 2023 at the hands of Rhysida saw the organization refuse to pay the criminals' 20 Bitcoin ransom demand, opting instead to drain its cash reserves and fork out millions for an IT rebuild . Although the library's response to the attack drew widespread praise, few institutions of its kind are in a financial position to follow its lead. Other libraries might not be willing or able to commit to a recovery period as lengthy as that of the British Library . In its 2025/26 annual report , published in July, the institution said its recovery is still incomplete, and work to fully restore customers' ability to purchase electronic resources, such as journals and research databases, and reopen access to electronic legal deposit content is ongoing. This is likely to be completed by the end of 2026, the British Library added. ®

item.title: Early Black Friday beginner telescope deal — this portable Celestron is now 25% off at Amazon
item.description:
Harry joined Space.com in December 2024 as an e-commerce staff writer covering cameras, optics, and skywatching content. Based in the UK, Harry graduated in 2019 with a Bachelor's degree in American Literature with Creative Writing from the University of East Anglia. A keen photographer, Harry has strong experience with astrophotography and has captured celestial objects with a range of cameras. As a lifelong skywatcher, Harry remembers watching the Perseid meteor shower every summer in his hometown and being amazed by the wonders of the night sky.

Black Friday is still weeks away but we've spotted this early telescope deal on a Celestron telescope designed with beginners in mind. The Celestron Travel Scope 70 is a great entry-level telescope that delivers better views of the moon, planets and some deep-sky objects. It's also suitable for children while you decide if you want to drop serious money on a bigger telescope further down the line. You can buy the Celestron Travel Scope 70, on sale right now for $90 on Amazon. Save $30 on this super-portable and beginner telescope that offers quality views and can be packed away into the supplied backpack. It boasts two eyepieces, which is enough to get someone started on their astronomy journey. We reviewed the Moon Mission Travel Scope 70 , which is essentially the same telescope with a lunar-themed skin. item.title: Meet Clara Serrajordi: Barcelona’s midfield hope filling the void left by Alexia Putellas | Moving the Goalposts
item.description: The 18-year-old on being thrown in at the deep end with the first team, playing with her idols and replacing a legend The next move on the chess board could not have been clearer for Barcelona and their coach, Pere Romeu: a new queen has broken into the Blaugrana midfield. Clara Serrajordi has made substantial moves already: she made her first-team debut at the age of 17, started ahead of Aitana Bonmatí in the 2026 Champions League final and is filling the void left by the departed Alexia Putellas this season. Serrajordi is a keen chess player and uses it to disconnect from football and there are similarities to how she plays. item.title: Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen
item.description: Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal. Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected." The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations. In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues. Torger Kjeldstad, director of digitalization at Norad, said "the attack is complex," and confirmed the agency has initiated a crisis team to manage it. "We know a lot about what has happened, but to ensure that we have a complete overview of the attack, we are working to engage external experts in cybersecurity," he said. "They will give us a detailed description of what information those who attacked the solution have gained access to." Kjeldstad added that "it should be safe" to continue using Norad's services while it continues to probe what happened, and who was behind it. Norad did not reveal many details about how the attack unfolded, other than saying that 27 accounts were compromised and were then used to gain access to the portal and the data in question. The agency said the intrusion was detected on October 30, but did not offer any indication as to how long the attackers retained access to the grant portal. It also refused to rule out that names of applicants in "conflict areas and authoritarian states" may have been included in the stolen data – it is not known if recipients would have also been registered users – and said it is approaching the matter "very seriously." The grant portal, managed by Norad, which itself is part of Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is responsible for handling applications from organizations across the world. Recent case studies include support for independent, investigative journalism in Moldova, a country which routinely battles Russian propaganda and election interference, and backing for Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. The issues Norad and the Norwegian government support, however, are wide-ranging – from access to healthcare for transgender people worldwide and Kenyan incubators for innovative transport solutions, to delivering aid to war-torn Gaza. ®

item.title: U.S. Consulate General Highlights Fashion’s Role in Expanding U.S.-Nigeria Commercial Ties During Lagos Fashion Week
item.description: U.S. Consul General Brandon Hudspeth delivering remarks at the event hosted at the Consul General’s residence in Lagos. Consulate General Lagos recently recognized the contributions of Lagos Fashion Week founder Omoyemi Akerele at a lunch held at the height of Lagos Fashion Week 2026. The event recognized Akerele’s vision in connecting Nigerian designers with American consumers and creating new opportunities for U.S. businesses. The occasion brought together designers, entrepreneurs, and creative leaders to highlight fashion’s role in strengthening U.S.-Nigeria ties. “It’s an honor to celebrate Lagos Fashion Week 2026 with so many of Nigeria’s most talented designers and creative leaders. For 15 years, Omoyemi has built one of Africa’s premier fashion showcases, connecting Nigerian designers with American buyers and retailers and showing how trade creates opportunity for both our countries,” said U.S. Consul General Brandon Hudspeth . In attendance was also award-winning American-born actress and producer Osas Ighodaro . Guests also experienced a new fashion themed game developed by Lagos based Maliyo Games, highlighting fashion’s growing links with technology and entertainment. Lagos Fashion Week founder Omoyemi Akerele speaking at the event hosted by the U.S. Consul General in her honor, celebrating her vision in connecting Nigerian designers with American consumers and creating new opportunities for U.S. businesses. Fashion is a major global industry, supporting jobs and commercial activity across design, retail, and related sectors including in both the United States and Nigeria. U.S. consumers spent an estimated $560 billion on clothing and footwear in 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. For Nigeria’s fashion industry, access to the American market offers a pathway to expand the reach of Nigerian designers while offering entry points into Africa for U.S. retailers and businesses. Since founding Lagos Fashion Week in 2011, Omoyemi Akerele has built the platform into one of Africa’s leading fashion showcases. Its 2025 edition featured more than 60 designers and welcomed approximately 15,000 guests. Lagos Fashion Week (LFW) has also become a bridge to the American fashion industry. Leading American singer Ciara walked the LFW runway in 2025, while Studio 189, the label co-founded by American actress Rosario Dawson , has shown collections in Lagos. New York-based Nigerian designer Tia Adeola has also featured her collections at LFW as well as American media outlets including Vogue and Essence being among the leading U.S. outlets that have covered the shows. LFW helps Nigerian designers explore the U.S. market through trade shows such as Coterie and NYNOW in New York and Liberty Fairs in Miami. Luxury retailer Moda Operandi has offered LFW designers access to American shoppers, while The Folklore, founded by American entrepreneur Amira Rasool, links African brands with U.S. buyers including through its partnership with Nordst

item.title: SAP promises to open out data flows in both directions
item.description: SAP has taken meaningful steps in opening its data to bidrectional sharing across the enterprise, and in decoupling the advanced analytics needed for AI from its ERP upgrade path. During a technical conference last week, the German software giant adopted native support for Apache Iceberg, the open table format, and extended its partnership with Databricks to bring data from legacy ERP systems into its modern cloud analytics platform. "By putting [a] stake in the ground with Iceberg, we now have SAP moving from a very closed application storage model to an open lakehouse model," said Aaron Rosenbaum, Gartner senior director analyst, referring to the concept which brings together data lakes and warehouses. Also important was the bridge between modern analytics in the cloud and on-prem or hosted legacy systems such as ECC, the ERP system broadly adopted by global companies. "SAP made a pretty big move in saying we're going to open this up, not just to S/4HANA Cloud [the latest ERP system], but ECC users. That coupling — leveraging of AI, leveraging a lakehouse for AI to the ERP upgrade lifecycle — was a problem," said Rosenbaum. In May this year, SAP bought Dremio, a lakehouse platform built around Apache Iceberg, ending its previous preference for Databricks' Delta Sharing to bring together SAP data products with existing lakehouses bi-directionally. At SAP's TedEd conference last week, SAP said its Business Data Cloud (BDC) – the "trusted data foundation for SAP Business AI Platform" – would now support native Apache Iceberg and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris, "providing an open and governed data foundation for users and [AI agent platform] Joule to consume data." Together with SAP BDC Connect, the new tech policy will support platform interoperability with "zero-copy data sharing" across platforms from Databricks, Snowflake, Google, AWS, and Microsoft. The system would also continue to support Delta Lake, the alternative open table format from Databricks, SAP said . With the integration of Dremio's SQL query engine, BDC users will also get access to relational databases including SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without moving data, the vendor said. During the same conference, Databricks – the lakehouse company born out of an Apache Spark platform – extended its partnership with SAP based on the previously announced SAP Databricks, which embeds the Databricks Data + AI Platform in BDC. That "expanded scope" promises to make data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. The vendor said that a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, for example, could use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring historic order data into SAP Databricks, combining it with third-party data, and allowing data engineers to build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines. item.dc:creator: Lindsay Clark
item.content:encoded: SAP has taken meaningful steps in opening its data to bidrectional sharing across the enterprise, and in decoupling the advanced analytics needed for AI from its ERP upgrade path. During a technical conference last week, the German software giant adopted native support for Apache Iceberg, the open table format, and extended its partnership with Databricks to bring data from legacy ERP systems into its modern cloud analytics platform. "By putting [a] stake in the ground with Iceberg, we now have SAP moving from a very closed application storage model to an open lakehouse model," said Aaron Rosenbaum, Gartner senior director analyst, referring to the concept which brings together data lakes and warehouses. Also important was the bridge between modern analytics in the cloud and on-prem or hosted legacy systems such as ECC, the ERP system broadly adopted by global companies. "SAP made a pretty big move in saying we're going to open this up, not just to S/4HANA Cloud [the latest ERP system], but ECC users. That coupling — leveraging of AI, leveraging a lakehouse for AI to the ERP upgrade lifecycle — was a problem," said Rosenbaum. In May this year, SAP bought Dremio, a lakehouse platform built around Apache Iceberg, ending its previous preference for Databricks' Delta Sharing to bring together SAP data products with existing lakehouses bi-directionally. At SAP's TedEd conference last week, SAP said its Business Data Cloud (BDC) – the "trusted data foundation for SAP Business AI Platform" – would now support native Apache Iceberg and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris, "providing an open and governed data foundation for users and [AI agent platform] Joule to consume data." Together with SAP BDC Connect, the new tech policy will support platform interoperability with "zero-copy data sharing" across platforms from Databricks, Snowflake, Google, AWS, and Microsoft. The system would also continue to support Delta Lake, the alternative open table format from Databricks, SAP said . With the integration of Dremio's SQL query engine, BDC users will also get access to relational databases including SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without moving data, the vendor said. During the same conference, Databricks – the lakehouse company born out of an Apache Spark platform – extended its partnership with SAP based on the previously announced SAP Databricks, which embeds the Databricks Data + AI Platform in BDC. That "expanded scope" promises to make data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. The vendor said that a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, for example, could use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring historic order data into SAP Databricks, combining it with third-party data, and allowing data engineers to build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines. They can keep that work as they move to the cloud, Databricks suggested . This being 2026, the hoped-for output from all of this data engineering is not just business insight, but automated action, by way of AI agents. SAP has its Joule AI assistant and agentic platform, while Databricks has Genie , and the two companies have promised to bring them together. The increasing openness is good for users who will get more options in plotting a strategy to bring together enterprise data, leaving them pondering over where to put the business context layer, which vendors will no doubt fight to control, Rosenbaum said. "You have the comment that they're going to bring Joule and Genie together in the future. This is pointing to a struggle that's going on throughout enterprises and throughout all the vendors about the context layer. I don't necessarily see that there's one winner. You do have different points of context within the transaction system and across the whole business, and they have been points of tension. "Lack of single vendor lock-in is important. It's something that all the customers are struggling with: how do we build these context layers and deliver sort of consistent answers?" SAP's shift in the direction of openness is likely to help users in this struggle, whether they choose to build the context layer within the ERP vendor's data platform using its semantic layer, or outside of it using tools from other vendors – there are plenty of companies offering help for those opening their wallets. Nonetheless, whichever path users choose, a lot of work lies ahead. ®

item.title: ‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto
item.description: As GTA 6 looms, we look at the films that have influenced Rockstar’s creatives, from Heat to Bonnie and Clyde, via Boyz n the Hood and Speed Grand Theft Auto is arguably the most cinematic video game series ever made. Over the past three decades, the games have studied and stolen the themes, conventions and visual dynamism of great gangster and action movies, applying them to open worlds filled with low-life characters and grand set-piece possibilities. Here then are the movies (and TV show) that have shaped the GTA experience, from the 1996 original to this year’s inescapable instalment. Continue reading...

item.title: Royal London plans IT outsourcing shake-up as staff brace for redundancies
item.description: Royal London plans to cut hundreds of IT jobs and shift work to India under an outsourcing deal with IBM, according to sources, with redundancies expected by the end of December. Sources said Royal London's chief technology officer, James Sandell, told IT staff in September that the insurance and pensions giant was partnering with IBM to outsource a substantial portion of its technology operations. A consultation process was expected to follow. A Royal London spokesperson told The Register : "Royal London has appointed IBM as its strategic technology infrastructure partner as it continues to develop its technology strategy. The partnership will give Royal London access to IBM’s specialist capability, scale and experience. Royal London will remain accountable for service delivery and regulatory requirements and continues to focus on ensuring continuity and quality of service for customers." We asked Royal London how many UK IT roles it would retain and whether IBM would move work to India. The exact number of jobs at risk remains unclear, although one Glassdoor review posted on October 6 claims that hundreds of positions in the company's technology operations division are being eliminated. "A vast amount of knowledge is being lost by the business, a lot that is not yet documented due to constant years of recruitment freeze and workload volume," they wrote. The reviewer also questioned whether management had grasped just how much work would be involved in handing operations over to IBM, particularly with already stretched teams being cut to a fraction of their former size. Royal London replied to the Glassdoor review, acknowledging staff concerns about the changes, though it didn't comment on the claims about outsourcing and redundancies. "We recognise that as Royal London is going through a period of transformation, this has raised questions and concerns for some colleagues," the company wrote. "We have established channels for colleagues to raise these, including through People Leaders and Colleague Representatives, and I encourage colleagues to use these routes to discuss their concerns." Other October reviews questioned the handling of the outsourcing and Royal London's commitment to its mutual values. An October 12 reviewer identifying themselves as an IT infrastructure employee said the company had historically offered good career prospects, before criticizing its new direction. "Sudden outsourcing goes against all Royal London values," the reviewer wrote, adding that employees were questioning the company's direction amid reports of a hiring freeze and further potential cuts. Another review, posted on October 20, suggested the IBM deal was the latest in a series of outsourcing decisions following an earlier move to transfer servicing jobs to South Africa. "A mutual company but not mutual values when it comes to things like this," the reviewer claimed. The planned cuts follow rising profits. Royal London reported adjusted group operating prof

item.content:encoded: Royal London plans to cut hundreds of IT jobs and shift work to India under an outsourcing deal with IBM, according to sources, with redundancies expected by the end of December. Sources said Royal London's chief technology officer, James Sandell, told IT staff in September that the insurance and pensions giant was partnering with IBM to outsource a substantial portion of its technology operations. A consultation process was expected to follow. A Royal London spokesperson told The Register : "Royal London has appointed IBM as its strategic technology infrastructure partner as it continues to develop its technology strategy. The partnership will give Royal London access to IBM’s specialist capability, scale and experience. Royal London will remain accountable for service delivery and regulatory requirements and continues to focus on ensuring continuity and quality of service for customers." We asked Royal London how many UK IT roles it would retain and whether IBM would move work to India. The exact number of jobs at risk remains unclear, although one Glassdoor review posted on October 6 claims that hundreds of positions in the company's technology operations division are being eliminated. "A vast amount of knowledge is being lost by the business, a lot that is not yet documented due to constant years of recruitment freeze and workload volume," they wrote. The reviewer also questioned whether management had grasped just how much work would be involved in handing operations over to IBM, particularly with already stretched teams being cut to a fraction of their former size. Royal London replied to the Glassdoor review, acknowledging staff concerns about the changes, though it didn't comment on the claims about outsourcing and redundancies. "We recognise that as Royal London is going through a period of transformation, this has raised questions and concerns for some colleagues," the company wrote. "We have established channels for colleagues to raise these, including through People Leaders and Colleague Representatives, and I encourage colleagues to use these routes to discuss their concerns." Other October reviews questioned the handling of the outsourcing and Royal London's commitment to its mutual values. An October 12 reviewer identifying themselves as an IT infrastructure employee said the company had historically offered good career prospects, before criticizing its new direction. "Sudden outsourcing goes against all Royal London values," the reviewer wrote, adding that employees were questioning the company's direction amid reports of a hiring freeze and further potential cuts. Another review, posted on October 20, suggested the IBM deal was the latest in a series of outsourcing decisions following an earlier move to transfer servicing jobs to South Africa. "A mutual company but not mutual values when it comes to things like this," the reviewer claimed. The planned cuts follow rising profits. Royal London reported adjusted group operating profit of £187 million in the first half of 2026, up 13 percent year-on-year. Royal London has been keen to trumpet the benefits of its mutual structure, under which it is owned by customers rather than shareholders. Reporting the results in August, chief executive Barry O'Dwyer highlighted the £199 million distributed to eligible customers through ProfitShare in April. "As a customer-owned business, when we do well, our customers share in that success," O'Dwyer said. For employees facing redundancy before Christmas, the benefits of that success may be somewhat harder to appreciate. The Reg has asked IBM to comment. ®

item.title: In Gallery: More Than The AI Conversations – See Moments From Goalkeepers Dakar 2026
item.description: In Dakar, for Goalkeepers 2026 , professionals from various industries converged in a hall on the 29th of October, 2026, to discuss how Africans are already leveraging AI to solve social problems, and to also explore further opportunities. Themed “ Equitable AI and the Future of African Youth “, the conversations weren’t all about using AI to build an equitable future; there were performances, including one from the legendary Youssou N’Dour , and the attendees also showed up and showed out in different styles and fashions. The event was attended by several influential figures, including Nigeria’s Tsakute Ladi Jonah (popularly known as Saskay), Fatou Jupiter Toure , Mamadou Ly , and Fatma Samoura , the former diplomat and senior executive who became the first female Secretary General of FIFA. Other notable attendees included Karim Sy , the entrepreneur and founder of Jokkolabs, and Dr Seydina Ndiaye , an AI expert at the UN High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence and the principal investigator of the AI Living Lab for Innovative and Viable Ethical Policies and Systems (ALIVE Lab), among others. item.title: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?
item.description: Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires. The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn. Continue reading...

item.title: 2 astronauts will finish upgrading ISS solar arrays during spacewalk today: Watch it live
item.description: null Two spacewalking astronauts will finish upgrading the International Space Station's power system today (Nov. 5), and you can watch the action live. NASA astronaut Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency 's Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) today, during a roughly seven-hour spacewalk that's scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT). You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 7 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT). NASA astronaut Anil Menon points his camera toward his spacesuit’s helmet visor and takes a selfie during a spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) Today's extravehicular activity (EVA) will be the second in a week for Menon and Kutryk, who installed the station's seventh iROSA during an Oct. 29 spacewalk . That excursion was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the ISS to date, and the first EVA for a Canadian astronaut since 2019. Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off. "The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3) . That's a boost of about 30%. Menon and Kutryk are currently sharing the ISS with five other astronauts — NASA's Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov. Delaney, Kutryk, Teteryatnikov and Watkins arrived at the ISS on Oct. 1, on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission . Dubrov, Kikina and Menon got there in mid-July, aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

item.title: Dayo Akinbode: What Travelling to Cuba Taught Me About Money
item.description: I went to Cuba for the salsa, the cigars, the rum and those gorgeous vintage cars. I never imagined that, somewhere between admiring the colourful streets and enjoying the Caribbean sunshine, I would receive an unexpected lesson in money management. Looking back, I can laugh about my experience. But at the time, discovering how much I might have been overpaying left me wondering how much my ignorance had already cost me. Cuba had a way of making me feel as though I had stepped into a film. Imagine standing in a sun-drenched plaza, a Cuban cigar in your hand, the warm Caribbean breeze brushing against your skin, and music floating through the air. Around you, buildings painted in faded yellows, dusty pinks and weathered blues stand proudly, their grand colonial facades and ornate balconies carrying stories from another century. Then comes the rumble of an engine. You turn to see a cherry-red vintage car gliding past, followed by a bubblegum-pink beauty that seems to have driven straight out of the 1950s. Everywhere you look, vibrant colours, rich history and lively movement bring the streets to life And the cars! Oh, the cars! Later, I would find myself riding in a neon-green convertible along the coast, the wind whipping through my hair as the blue Caribbean Sea stretched beside me. I felt wonderfully alive. Cuba was giving me everything I had hoped for: beauty, music, history and the thrill of discovering somewhere different. I was so captivated by everything that I paid little attention to the money in my purse. I visited Cuba in 2019, when the country had two official currencies: the Cuban convertible peso, known as the CUC, and the Cuban peso, known as the CUP. To an unsuspecting tourist like me, this arrangement was a recipe for confusion. I was carrying CUC notes, commonly used by visitors because that is what the banks give you in exchange for your USD notes. The CUC notes looked different from the CUP notes I would later encounter. CUC notes featured monuments, while CUP notes carried the faces of Cuban national heroes, including José Martí and Camilo Cienfuegos. But at the time, I barely noticed the distinction. Money was money, or so I thought. Whenever I needed to pay for something, I reached into my purse, brought out my CUC notes and settled the bill. I was enjoying my holiday and had no reason to suspect my wallet was quietly making it more expensive than necessary. Then, one time, I was given change in a currency different from the familiar CUC. I looked at the notes in my hand and immediately felt that something was wrong. These were not the notes I was accustomed to using. I did not recognise them, and I was not about to walk away with money I did not understand. So, I rejected the change. Imagine my surprise when the cashier and another customer explained to me that the notes were perfectly valid Cuban money! That was when I got my crash course in Cuban economics. item.dc:creator: Dayo Akinbode
item.content:encoded: I went to Cuba for the salsa, the cigars, the rum and those gorgeous vintage cars. I never imagined that, somewhere between admiring the colourful streets and enjoying the Caribbean sunshine, I would receive an unexpected lesson in money management. Looking back, I can laugh about my experience. But at the time, discovering how much I might have been overpaying left me wondering how much my ignorance had already cost me. Cuba had a way of making me feel as though I had stepped into a film. Imagine standing in a sun-drenched plaza, a Cuban cigar in your hand, the warm Caribbean breeze brushing against your skin, and music floating through the air. Around you, buildings painted in faded yellows, dusty pinks and weathered blues stand proudly, their grand colonial facades and ornate balconies carrying stories from another century. Then comes the rumble of an engine. You turn to see a cherry-red vintage car gliding past, followed by a bubblegum-pink beauty that seems to have driven straight out of the 1950s. Everywhere you look, vibrant colours, rich history and lively movement bring the streets to life And the cars! Oh, the cars! Later, I would find myself riding in a neon-green convertible along the coast, the wind whipping through my hair as the blue Caribbean Sea stretched beside me. I felt wonderfully alive. Cuba was giving me everything I had hoped for: beauty, music, history and the thrill of discovering somewhere different. I was so captivated by everything that I paid little attention to the money in my purse. I visited Cuba in 2019, when the country had two official currencies: the Cuban convertible peso, known as the CUC, and the Cuban peso, known as the CUP. To an unsuspecting tourist like me, this arrangement was a recipe for confusion. I was carrying CUC notes, commonly used by visitors because that is what the banks give you in exchange for your USD notes. The CUC notes looked different from the CUP notes I would later encounter. CUC notes featured monuments, while CUP notes carried the faces of Cuban national heroes, including José Martí and Camilo Cienfuegos. But at the time, I barely noticed the distinction. Money was money, or so I thought. Whenever I needed to pay for something, I reached into my purse, brought out my CUC notes and settled the bill. I was enjoying my holiday and had no reason to suspect my wallet was quietly making it more expensive than necessary. Then, one time, I was given change in a currency different from the familiar CUC. I looked at the notes in my hand and immediately felt that something was wrong. These were not the notes I was accustomed to using. I did not recognise them, and I was not about to walk away with money I did not understand. So, I rejected the change. Imagine my surprise when the cashier and another customer explained to me that the notes were perfectly valid Cuban money! That was when I got my crash course in Cuban economics. The country had two official currencies: the Cuban convertible peso (CUC), and the Cuban peso (CUP). I was carrying CUC notes, commonly used by visitors. The notes I had just rejected were CUP notes, used by the locals. I was relieved, slightly embarrassed and suddenly very curious. How had I been in Cuba for four days without understanding something so fundamental to paying for things? The top notes (CUC) have monuments and are for tourists. The bottom notes (CUP) have national heroes and are for locals. Suddenly, I began wondering how much I had already spent and how I had been paying far more than necessary. I recalled tipping a tour guide 10 CUC. He had been delighted, even asking me whether I was sure I wanted to give him that much. At the time, I thought I was simply being generous. But after learning that the commonly used conversion was around 25 CUP to 1 CUC, I understood why he might have been so pleased. My tip was equivalent to about 250 CUP. I did not regret rewarding someone for good service, but I was beginning to understand how easily a visitor could spend money without appreciating its value. Then came the experience that really opened my eyes. I had been eating at a particular local food joint and paying 5 CUC for my meal because the menu read $5. I always enjoyed the food and always handed over 5 CUC because 1 USD was equivalent to 1 CUC. But now that I knew about CUP, curiosity got the better of me. On my next visit, I decided to observe before ordering. A local customer arrived ahead of me. I waited and watched what he ordered, how much he paid and which notes he handed to the cashier. Five CUP. Five CUP? I watched him complete his transaction and leave. Then I stepped forward and ordered the same meal. When the time came to pay, I brought out my newly acquired CUP notes and handed over 5 CUP. The cashier raised an eyebrow. I pointed to the menu and explained that I had just watched the customer before me order the same meal and pay the same amount. I was not guessing. I got my meal for 5 CUP as against the 5 CUC I had always paid. At the commonly used conversion rate of 25 CUP to 1 CUC, my previous payment of 5 CUC was equivalent to 125 CUP. I had been paying 125 CUP for a meal that I had just watched a local buy for a mere 5 CUP Twenty-five times the price! I was stunned. Part of me wanted to laugh at the absurdity of it all; another part wondered how many other times I had paid without understanding the difference. I had been so confident, so comfortable reaching into my purse and handing over my money. Yet I had missed a detail that could make a significant difference to my spending. That local joint visit became one of my most memorable Cuban experiences. Not because of the food, but because of the lesson I had been taught. Of course, my story is about Cuba in 2019. The currency system has since changed. On 1 January 2021, Cuba discontinued the CUC as part of a currency reform, leaving the Cuban peso (CUP) as the sole official currency. The two-currency arrangement that caught me off guard belongs to that chapter of the country’s history. What remains with me, however, is not just the currency confusion. I remember Cuba’s faded pastel buildings, the vintage cars gleaming beneath the sun, the music in the streets and the thrill of driving along the coast in that neon-green convertible. The country was vibrant, beautiful and full of contrasts. But whenever I travel somewhere new, I remind myself to ask questions, understand the local currency, and never assume I know how things work. The post Dayo Akinbode: What Travelling to Cuba Taught Me About Money appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Uefa faces political flashpoint over Sevastopol’s ascent in Russian football
item.description: Promotion to third tier for Crimean club would be clear violation of governing body’s rules amid conflict in Ukraine Uefa and Fifa face a decisive test of their appetite to punish Russia’s integration of teams from illegally occupied Ukrainian territory after FC Sevastopol, from Crimea, won promotion to the country’s professional third tier. Sevastopol were declared champions of group one in Football National League (FNL) 2B, in effect Russia’s fourth division, last month and are believed to have applied for a licence to compete at the level above. Should it be granted and they proceed to FNL 2A, it would appear a violation of Uefa rules that prohibit Crimean clubs from playing in competitions organised by the Russian Football Union (RFU). The governing body would come under severe pressure to extend sanctions on European football’s pariah state, whose club and national teams are banned from competing in international tournaments. Continue reading...

item.title: Apple iPad mini A20 Pro review: the best small tablet but with a big price
item.description: All-round upgrades fit a bigger OLED screen in a smaller and lighter body with water resistance for first time The new iPad mini takes Apple’s fan-favourite tiny tablet and upgrades just about everything about it, including giving it a new OLED screen, serious performance, speakers embedded into the display and even water resistance, all with a big new price tag. The eighth-generation iPad mini costs from £699 (€749/$699/A$1,099), which is £200 or equivalent more than the original price of its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to bite . That makes it uncomfortably expensive, costing £270 more than the base model iPad (A16) and only £50 cheaper than the bigger 11in iPad Air M4 . Continue reading...

item.title: When datacenters lose power, generators should kick in. That didn’t happen for Google in London
item.description: Google Cloud has revealed that the cause of the October 20 outage in its europe-west-2-b availability zone was a ‘misconfiguration’ of its systems that meant its emergency generators didn’t start. The outage at the London facility caused service interruptions at outfits including Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and Revolut . In a November 4 update to its service status page, Google explained what went wrong. “The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture — where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load — backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC),” Google revealed. The facility gets its juice from two independent utility feeders, which Google calls “A” and “B”. There’s also a “standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events.” Google says the root cause of the incident was failure in an external underground cable through which its power supplier brings ‘leccy to its bit barns. That cable connects to primary feeder A and it broke at a time when feeder B wasn’t working. “Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026,” Google admitted. “Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.” That shouldn’t be a problem for a top-tier operator like Google, which knows it needs to install backup sources of electricity like uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and on-site generators. Indeed, europe-west-2-b employs UPSes that Google says can keep things up and running for five minutes if the availability zone loses its connection to the grid. The UPSes worked, but a “voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load.” Google’s UPSes therefore ran out of juice, but its generators didn’t start. The rest is history. The search giant has figured out that its PLCs weren’t set up to handle the conditions it faced on this fateful day. “PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant,” the status update reveals. Once Google was able to reconnect to its power utility, it reprogrammed the PLC so it wouldn’t make the same mistake again. The Big G has since made many changes to the electrical setup at europe-west-2-b and says it’s tested them and that they all work. item.content:encoded: Google Cloud has revealed that the cause of the October 20 outage in its europe-west-2-b availability zone was a ‘misconfiguration’ of its systems that meant its emergency generators didn’t start. The outage at the London facility caused service interruptions at outfits including Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and Revolut . In a November 4 update to its service status page, Google explained what went wrong. “The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture — where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load — backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC),” Google revealed. The facility gets its juice from two independent utility feeders, which Google calls “A” and “B”. There’s also a “standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events.” Google says the root cause of the incident was failure in an external underground cable through which its power supplier brings ‘leccy to its bit barns. That cable connects to primary feeder A and it broke at a time when feeder B wasn’t working. “Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026,” Google admitted. “Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.” That shouldn’t be a problem for a top-tier operator like Google, which knows it needs to install backup sources of electricity like uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and on-site generators. Indeed, europe-west-2-b employs UPSes that Google says can keep things up and running for five minutes if the availability zone loses its connection to the grid. The UPSes worked, but a “voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load.” Google’s UPSes therefore ran out of juice, but its generators didn’t start. The rest is history. The search giant has figured out that its PLCs weren’t set up to handle the conditions it faced on this fateful day. “PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant,” the status update reveals. Once Google was able to reconnect to its power utility, it reprogrammed the PLC so it wouldn’t make the same mistake again. The Big G has since made many changes to the electrical setup at europe-west-2-b and says it’s tested them and that they all work. It’s also given itself two action items, one of which it describes as a “Communications Enhancement” that will see it “bolster notification speed by developing an automated alert-to-communication mechanism for location-impacting incidents.” The other is to “expand platform-wide testing outcomes for infrastructure-level events.” Once Google gets that done, perhaps it will be able to handle outages better – and if not, at least advise customers about its troubles more quickly. ®

item.title: VMware quietly offers European users extended sales and support for low-end vSphere
item.description: VMware appears to have made a concession to European regulators by extending the life of its low-end vSphere Standard and Enterprise Plus products. The virtualization pioneer quietly announced the extension in the November 4 blog post in which it announced a new low-end product called vSphere Express , which The Register reported yesterday. We based our report about vSphere Express on an interview, and on material provided by VMware – which sent a version of the blog post linked to above. The version we saw did not include the following paragraph, the contents of which were not mentioned in our interview: “Furthermore, for customers in countries in the European Economic Area, vSphere Standard version 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus version 8 will remain available for sale until October 31, 2027, and will have Extended Support included in any active subscriptions to those offerings until the earlier of the applicable subscription end date or October 31, 2028.” The latter date is more than a year past the October 11, 2027, end-of-general-support date for the more capable vSphere 8 and Cloud Foundation 5.x products. “This has the potential to be a positive development for organisations within the European Economic Area,” independent analyst Michael Warrilow told The Register . “It could provide them up to an extra 12 months to transition vSphere 8 to VCF 9 and/or migrate workloads to another platform.” Warrilow thinks European users should seek “absolute clarity” from VMware about the specifics of its offer. “What level of extended support will be provided and what longer-term commitments will need to be made? I cannot find any of that detail,” he wrote. A reminder: VMware has promised in the past to make patches available for users who choose to persist with perpetual licenses instead of moving to its preferred subscriptions. The Broadcom business unit later paused patch downloads for months, claiming it needed to adjust its website to make them possible. Warrilow wonders why VMware will keep selling vSphere Standard only in Europe and suggested “regulatory muscle” is the reason. Regulators around the world cleared Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware. In Europe, authorities have since revisited the matter. Lobby group Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe (CISPE) has succeeded in having the European Commission open an antitrust investigation into whether VMware’s channel changes inappropriately shaped the cloud infrastructure provider market. The Register understands CISPE feels regulators are receptive to its arguments. In the Netherlands, local courts enforced a VMware support contract of the sort that Broadcom has tried to walk away from at other users. Warrilow wonders if VMware might now change its policy regarding vSphere Standard in other countries. “The subsequent question is how can organisations in other regions get the same concessions from Broadcom? item.content:encoded: VMware appears to have made a concession to European regulators by extending the life of its low-end vSphere Standard and Enterprise Plus products. The virtualization pioneer quietly announced the extension in the November 4 blog post in which it announced a new low-end product called vSphere Express , which The Register reported yesterday. We based our report about vSphere Express on an interview, and on material provided by VMware – which sent a version of the blog post linked to above. The version we saw did not include the following paragraph, the contents of which were not mentioned in our interview: “Furthermore, for customers in countries in the European Economic Area, vSphere Standard version 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus version 8 will remain available for sale until October 31, 2027, and will have Extended Support included in any active subscriptions to those offerings until the earlier of the applicable subscription end date or October 31, 2028.” The latter date is more than a year past the October 11, 2027, end-of-general-support date for the more capable vSphere 8 and Cloud Foundation 5.x products. “This has the potential to be a positive development for organisations within the European Economic Area,” independent analyst Michael Warrilow told The Register . “It could provide them up to an extra 12 months to transition vSphere 8 to VCF 9 and/or migrate workloads to another platform.” Warrilow thinks European users should seek “absolute clarity” from VMware about the specifics of its offer. “What level of extended support will be provided and what longer-term commitments will need to be made? I cannot find any of that detail,” he wrote. A reminder: VMware has promised in the past to make patches available for users who choose to persist with perpetual licenses instead of moving to its preferred subscriptions. The Broadcom business unit later paused patch downloads for months, claiming it needed to adjust its website to make them possible. Warrilow wonders why VMware will keep selling vSphere Standard only in Europe and suggested “regulatory muscle” is the reason. Regulators around the world cleared Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware. In Europe, authorities have since revisited the matter. Lobby group Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe (CISPE) has succeeded in having the European Commission open an antitrust investigation into whether VMware’s channel changes inappropriately shaped the cloud infrastructure provider market. The Register understands CISPE feels regulators are receptive to its arguments. In the Netherlands, local courts enforced a VMware support contract of the sort that Broadcom has tried to walk away from at other users. Warrilow wonders if VMware might now change its policy regarding vSphere Standard in other countries. “The subsequent question is how can organisations in other regions get the same concessions from Broadcom? I would encourage them to amplify their voice by rallying industry associations and user groups to the cause whilst lobbying the regulators in their jurisdiction.” Overall, however, he thinks VMware’s decision isn’t enormously impactful. “Ultimately, all it does is buy a little more time to upgrade or migrate,” he wrote. It may not even do that, as The Register often heard that VMware seldom issued quotes for vSphere Standard or Enterprise Plus. Paul Turner, chief product officer for VMware’s Cloud Foundation Division, told The Register that inappropriate incentives for channel partners caused that situation, and that VMware later fixed it. Continental users will be hoping VMware got that effort right. ®

item.title: Microsoft admits certifications can be a drag, launches creds that recognize skills
item.description: When The Register writes about professional certifications offered by vendors, we often receive comments arguing that such credentials are nowhere near as valuable as real-world experience. Now, Microsoft has acknowledged there’s some merit in that argument. Redmond revealed its stance last week in a post from general manager for content and insights Cameron Percy, who observed: “For years, people have asked for a simpler way to prove the skills they use in the flow of work, without stepping away to prepare for another test.” Microsoft’s response is the “Pro Badge,” a new form of credential that Percy wrote “works alongside Microsoft Certifications.” “Certifications show that you can solve problems in a role or field. Pro Badge shows how you use a specific product in your everyday work. Together, they give a more complete picture of what you can do.” “Instead of capturing skills on a single test day, this approach keeps pace with your work and the products you use,” Percy added. “It gives you a current, verified signal of what you can do, at no cost and without a separate exam or study guide.” The first Pro Badge is for GitHub Copilot. To earn it, users need only visit learn.github.com and sign in with their GitHub account. Going through those steps fires up a “proficiency engine” that Microsoft says “gets to work analyzing relevant product usage signals and evaluating them against a defined proficiency framework.” Percy’s post says it “systematically uses evidence from everyday product use to calculate and automatically update your proficiency level.” Microsoft offers five levels of proficiency: beginner, intermediate, proficient, advanced, and expert. To earn a Pro Badge, users must reach the proficient level. A beginner has had “first contact” with GitHub and “understands what Copilot is, where it can be used, and how it might fit into everyday development workflows.” An intermediate user is “familiar with web-based collaboration features, core IDE features, model management, agent configuration, customization options, and techniques for managing context.” To score the Pro Badge, users will need to demonstrate “practical ability to work on projects” and use GitHub “across typical scenarios, demonstrated through consistent hands-on usage across multiple repositories and extended periods.” “A Proficient user can use many web and IDE features, select appropriate models, and apply customizations to tailor Copilot for specific project needs. They have experimented with extended features and are aware of extensibility/integration options.” At the time of writing, Redmond hasn’t defined expert or advanced proficiency. It has published more criteria for the first three levels here . Microsoft has kindly integrated GitHub’s learning site with LinkedIn, which it owns, so users can add Pro Badges to their profiles. item.content:encoded: When The Register writes about professional certifications offered by vendors, we often receive comments arguing that such credentials are nowhere near as valuable as real-world experience. Now, Microsoft has acknowledged there’s some merit in that argument. Redmond revealed its stance last week in a post from general manager for content and insights Cameron Percy, who observed: “For years, people have asked for a simpler way to prove the skills they use in the flow of work, without stepping away to prepare for another test.” Microsoft’s response is the “Pro Badge,” a new form of credential that Percy wrote “works alongside Microsoft Certifications.” “Certifications show that you can solve problems in a role or field. Pro Badge shows how you use a specific product in your everyday work. Together, they give a more complete picture of what you can do.” “Instead of capturing skills on a single test day, this approach keeps pace with your work and the products you use,” Percy added. “It gives you a current, verified signal of what you can do, at no cost and without a separate exam or study guide.” The first Pro Badge is for GitHub Copilot. To earn it, users need only visit learn.github.com and sign in with their GitHub account. Going through those steps fires up a “proficiency engine” that Microsoft says “gets to work analyzing relevant product usage signals and evaluating them against a defined proficiency framework.” Percy’s post says it “systematically uses evidence from everyday product use to calculate and automatically update your proficiency level.” Microsoft offers five levels of proficiency: beginner, intermediate, proficient, advanced, and expert. To earn a Pro Badge, users must reach the proficient level. A beginner has had “first contact” with GitHub and “understands what Copilot is, where it can be used, and how it might fit into everyday development workflows.” An intermediate user is “familiar with web-based collaboration features, core IDE features, model management, agent configuration, customization options, and techniques for managing context.” To score the Pro Badge, users will need to demonstrate “practical ability to work on projects” and use GitHub “across typical scenarios, demonstrated through consistent hands-on usage across multiple repositories and extended periods.” “A Proficient user can use many web and IDE features, select appropriate models, and apply customizations to tailor Copilot for specific project needs. They have experimented with extended features and are aware of extensibility/integration options.” At the time of writing, Redmond hasn’t defined expert or advanced proficiency. It has published more criteria for the first three levels here . Microsoft has kindly integrated GitHub’s learning site with LinkedIn, which it owns, so users can add Pro Badges to their profiles. Percy’s post suggests Microsoft has other Pro Badges in the works. Elsewhere, Microsoft makes it plain that Pro Badges won’t replace its other credentials. “GitHub Verified Proficiency is part of Microsoft Pro Badge, a new credential type designed to recognize skills as they are applied in the flow of work,” explains a page offering detail of the new cred. “It does not replace certifications or Microsoft Applied Skills. It adds a third signal: how skills show up through everyday product use.” The Register welcomes comment on this new approach to professional credentials. ®

item.title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
item.description: The tech billionaire set spending record as he poured $446m into campaigns for failed Republican candidates Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections . It turned out to be a poor investment. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending. Continue reading...

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
item.description: null On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms. After failing to launch this batch of cubesats, the Super Strypi program never recovered from its failure, and the Air Force never tried launching another one. The U.S. Air Force’s rail-launched Super Strypi rocket lifted off from Hawaii about 9:45 p.m. local time on Nov. 3, 2015,, roared toward the sky and failed less than a minute into the long-awaited flight. (Image credit: U.S. Air Force) Why it mattered The Super Strypi rocket was a 21st century take on a 1960s rocket. It was designed to be a modern version of the three-stage Strypi sounding rocket used for for reentry vehicle and anti-missile target tests. Its three stages, powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, was designed to reach orbit, rather than suborbital trajectories common to most sounding rockets. The U.S. Air Force hoped Super Strypi would be a new tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs. Altogether, it was designed to launch small payloads of up to 300 kilograms into space for a mere $15 million per mission . The rocket's primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, short for Operationally Responsive Space 4, which was built for the Air Force by engineers at the University of Hawaii (who nicknamed it HiakaSat). It was designed to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment over the course of a year. The 12 other payloads on Super Strypi included eight cubesats for NASA's Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission, and as well as four others for universities that had been added as secondary payloads. Since the Super Strypi failure, neither the Air Force or Space Force has opted to use the rocket for a new mission. The Space Force has turned instead to commercial companies for fast-turnaround launch support. In June of this year, the U.S. Space Force teamed up with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with just 17 hours of notice , a new record to demonstrate short-turnaround launch response. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Trump declares 'American space superiority for all eternity' in election night proclamation
item.description: null President Trump issued a declaration yesterday (Nov. 3), proclaiming space open to all humanity for exploration, and the right of American citizens to develop and settle the solar system according to United States laws. "The American Declaration of Freedom in Space," describes space as the "province of all humans" and asserts that the United States will lead humanity's expansion into the cosmos. The proclamation reiterates the administration's goals with NASA's Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 and eventually sending astronauts to Mars , but introduces no new funding, programs or policy directives. "Our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty," the document says. Trump invoked America's "frontier spirit," highlighting Apollo 11 astronauts as the first people in history to walk on the moon's surface and robotic rovers exploring Mars as examples of U.S. leadership, and emphasized the country's flourishing commercial space sector helping ensure "American space superiority for all eternity." "The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity," the declaration says, and pledges that America will carry the values of faith, freedom and individual liberty into an interplanetary civilization. The proclamation also highlights the success of NASA's Artemis II mission in April, which carried four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and set a record for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth . The follow-up to that mission, Artemis III, is scheduled to launch next summer (2027), and will test rendezvous and docking operations between NASA's Orion spacecraft and the program's two commercial lunar landers in low Earth orbit . Artemis IV will be the program's first lunar landing mission, and is targeted for 2028. A December 2025 executive order from the President reaffirmed the goal of meeting that timeline, as well as the deployment of the initial elements for a permanent lunar outpost by 2030. Trump's declaration yesterday does not establish new NASA programs, allocate additional funding or issue instructions to federal agencies. Its sweeping language, though, does echo some of the principles in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty , which guarantees freedom of exploration while prohibiting national sovereignty claims on other planets.

item.title: Upcoming Marvel movies and TV shows: Avengers: Doomsday, Secret Wars, X-Men & more
item.description: Marvel fatigue? Think again, especially after Spider-Man: Brand New Day made over $2.5 billion worldwide and Avengers: Doomsday is looking hot, hot, hot! But even after the uneven Multiverse Saga ends (hopefully on a high note), Marvel Studios won’t be stopping. So, we've put together a list of all the upcoming MCU movies and shows confirmed so far. While the MCU isn't stopping, Marvel has slowed its roll, with the powers that be returning to the “quality over quantity” approach that defined Marvel Studios’ Infinity Saga output. This means no more than three movies per year and, perhaps more importantly, severely cutting down on TV productions, with a focus on multi-season shows rather than limited series that should’ve been a movie. It’s a time of change for both Disney and Marvel, but it seems everyone agrees the big screen reigns supreme, so expect a thinner streaming output and more relevant movies starring characters you actually know. More will be revealed in due time, but for now, here’s what lies at the Multiverse Saga’s end and beyond... Spoilers ahead for the Marvel Cinematic Universe so far. Watch Marvel movies and shows on Disney+: Disney+ (With Ads): $11.99/month Disney+ Premium (No Ads): $18.99/month or $189.99/year Avengers: Doomsday — December 18, 2026 (Image credit: Marvel Studios) Release date: December 18, 2026 | Director: Anthony & Joe Russo | Cast: Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Pedro Pascal, Robert Downey Jr. Earth’s Mightiest Heroes (from different Earths, actually) are assembling again in December 2026. Avengers: Doomsday 's cast looks ridiculously stacked, and it’ll finally realize the dream of bringing together the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, and the X-Men (Fox’s original ones, that is) on the big screen. It’s a lot to absorb, and we don’t really know what's going on, but the trailers released so far are promising. Anthony & Joe Russo (Captain America: The Winter Soldier & Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War & Endgame) are returning to direct, so that’s a good reason to be hyped even if the duo’s post-Marvel career hasn’t been the most exciting. Stephen McFeely (one of their two go-to scribes) is also back, and Michael Waldron ( Loki ) is helping out as well. It’s an all-star team for the most ambitious MCU project to date, at least until it all culminates in... Daredevil: Born Again (Season 3) — March 2027 (Image credit: Marvel Studios) Release window: March 2027 | Showrunner: Dario Scardapane | Cast: Charlie Cox, Mike Colter, Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter Daredevil: Born Again’s debut season was far from perfect, but most viewers agreed that Season 2 was a marked improvement. Hopefully, that energy will continue in the third and final outing , as the Defenders reunite, with Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter, and Mike Colter all returning from their Netflix shows. Another shocker is the (unofficially) confirmed return of Elodie Yung’s Elektra. We suspect some of these characters will be transferred to movies post-Secre
